lines: Wind howls through a gap in the crystal walls, and suddenly you are above everything. The aerie clings to the Spire's exterior face like a balcony carved from living stone, overlooking the vast Nightside darkness.

This was an observation post — not for watching enemies, but for watching the sky. Crystal lenses set into the walls focus starlight into geometric patterns on the floor, star-maps that still update after millennia.
The raiders never found this place. The only access was across a gap they couldn't cross. But you can hover.

Wind howls through a gap in the crystal walls, and suddenly you are above everything. The aerie clings to the Spire's exterior face like a balcony carved from living stone, overlooking the vast Nightside darkness.

This was an observation post — not for watching enemies, but for watching the sky. Crystal lenses set into the walls focus starlight into geometric patterns on the floor, star-maps that still update after millennia.
The raiders never found this place. The only access was across a gap they couldn't cross. But you can hover.

The cache opens with a crystalline chime. Inside, nested in geometric packing material that crumbles at your touch, is an Underlumen component — dark-tuned, pulsing with the same frequency as the Nightside itself.
An Umbral Amplifier. The Vigil-keepers must have used these to boost their observation equipment. In your sol grid, it will massively amplify damage output.
This cache holds something different — not a component, but a record. A geometric tablet etched with patterns that shift as you turn it in the starlight.

The Vigil-keepers logged everything from this aerie. Star positions, atmospheric readings, and something else — resonance signatures from deep underground. The same frequencies the Underlumen network uses.

One entry stands out: a notation marking the moment the Vigil-keepers first detected an anomalous signal in the network. They couldn't identify its source. They marked it with a single symbol that translates roughly to 'not ours.'
The crystal lenses overhead project a shifting star-map onto the floor. The constellations are unfamiliar — the sky has changed since this map was calibrated.

But one feature remains constant: a bright point at the center of the projection, pulsing in sync with your sol unit. The Lighthouse network's anchor frequency, still broadcasting after all this time.
